title: Function overloading, templates, and default arguments
relevance: Interviewers probe whether candidates can write one conceptual operation for many argument shapes without illegal overload clashes, broken template deduction, or misuse of defaults.

phases.goal: Establish what overloading, function templates, and default arguments each allow.

must_hit.point: Two or more functions may share a name if their parameter lists differ in number of parameters or in types.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States overloads are distinguished by parameter lists (count and/or types), not by name alone.

must_hit.point: A function template writes the function once with a placeholder type parameter; the compiler generates a concrete version for each type actually used.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes one templated definition plus compiler instantiation per used type.

must_hit.point: A parameter may be given a default value, making it optional at the call site.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says a defaulted parameter can be omitted and the default is supplied instead.

probes: What three C++ features let one conceptual operation serve many argument shapes, and what does each one do?

hints.1: Think about same name with different signatures, one body for many types, and optional trailing parameters.
hints.2: Overloading shares a name across differing parameter lists; templates use a type parameter; defaults make a parameter optional.
hints.3: Overloads: same name, different parameters; template: placeholder type, compiler generates per use; default argument: optional at the call site.

phases.goal: Show how the compiler picks overloads, when return type fails as a distinguisher, how template deduction binds T, and where defaults may appear.

must_hit.point: The compiler selects the overload by matching the call’s arguments to the parameter lists.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions argument matching / call-site types and arity drive which overload is called.

must_hit.point: Overloads must differ in their parameters; differing only in return type is not a distinct overload and will not compile.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the clash of int max(int,int) vs float max(int,int) and says return type alone cannot disambiguate because the return may be ignored.

must_hit.point: With one template parameter T, both arguments must deduce to the same type; mixing float and double (e.g. maxim(2.3f, 5.6)) yields no matching function.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains T cannot be both float and double for one call, so mixed types fail deduction unless cast.

must_hit.point: Only trailing parameters may carry defaults so omitted arguments are always the last ones.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States defaults are restricted to trailing parameters for positional omission to work.

probes: Why is float max(int, int) illegal next to int max(int, int), and what goes wrong if you call a single-T maxim with a float and a double?

hints.1: Ask what the call site must supply for the compiler to choose, including when the return is unused.
hints.2: Return type is invisible if ignored; one T cannot bind two different argument types.
hints.3: Identical (int,int) parameters with different return types clash; maxim(2.3f, 5.6) fails because T cannot be both float and double.

phases.goal: Contrast when to use separate overloads, a template, or a defaulted parameter instead of another overload.

must_hit.point: When logic is identical across types and only the types change, separate hand-written overloads are wasteful compared with one template.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says one template replaces separate typed max/maxim overloads when the body is the same.

must_hit.point: A single function with a default argument can replace a pair of overloads that differ only by an optional trailing parameter.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Notes one add with z defaulted covers both two- and three-argument calls that would otherwise need two overloads.

probes: When would you prefer a template over typed overloads, and when does a default argument replace an overload pair?

hints.1: Compare identical logic across types versus optional last parameters with the same body.
hints.2: Same algorithm, different types → template; same algorithm, optional trailing arg → default.
hints.3: Template replaces int/float max-style overloads; defaulted z replaces separate add(int,int) and add(int,int,int).

phases.goal: Apply overload selection, template deduction, and defaulted calls to concrete call sites from the material.

must_hit.point: For overloaded add, add(a, b) uses the two-int version and add(a, b, c) uses the three-int version when a, b, c are ints.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the two- and three-argument int calls to the matching overloads.

must_hit.point: With int add(int x, int y, int z = 0), add(2, 5) yields 7, add(2, 5, 8) yields 15, and add(2, 5, 0) yields 7.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the three call results using the default or explicit z.

must_hit.point: maxim(12, 14) deduces T as int and maxim(2.3, 1.4) deduces T as double from matching argument types.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the deduced types for those two calls.

probes: Given the overloaded and defaulted add examples, what is called or returned for add(a,b), add(a,b,c), add(2,5), and add(2,5,8)?

hints.1: Match arity and types first; then apply the default when the last argument is omitted.
hints.2: Two ints → two-param overload; three ints → three-param; omitted z uses 0.
hints.3: add(a,b) two-int overload; add(a,b,c) three-int; add(2,5)→7; add(2,5,8)→15.

tradeoffs.topic: Function template vs hand-written typed overloads
tradeoffs.strong_answer: If the logic is identical and only the types change, one template with a type parameter replaces separate overloads such as int and float max; the compiler generates a concrete version per type actually used.

tradeoffs.topic: Default argument vs overload pair for optional trailing parameter
tradeoffs.strong_answer: One function with a trailing default (e.g. z = 0) often replaces writing both a two-parameter and a three-parameter overload when the body is the same.

gotchas.trap: Declaring two functions that differ only in return type (e.g. int max(int,int) and float max(int,int)) and treating them as overloads.
gotchas.correction: Overloads must differ in parameters; return type alone is not enough because a call may ignore the return, so the compiler has no basis to choose and the program will not compile.

gotchas.trap: Calling a single-parameter-type template like maxim with mixed argument types (e.g. float and double).
gotchas.correction: One T must resolve to a single type per call; both arguments must be the same type or be cast so deduction can succeed.

gotchas.trap: Putting default arguments on non-trailing parameters.
gotchas.correction: Only trailing parameters may carry defaults so that any omitted arguments are always the last ones.
